result.dimension: SCHEME extraction and the scheme/authority separator

rules.rule: The scheme/authority separator is the exact 3-byte literal "://". A bare ':' is NOT sufficient, and '//' without a preceding ':' is not sufficient. If "://" does not occur (in the searched region, see later rules), scheme is empty, host is empty, port is -1, and the ENTIRE remaining string becomes the path.

scheme = the substring strictly BEFORE the FIRST occurrence of "://". The remainder-parse (authority/host/port/path) begins at exactly separator_index + 3, i.e. immediately after the three separator bytes. Later "://" occurrences are never used as the separator.

There is NO validation of the scheme's characters. Any bytes at all may precede the "://" and all of them become the scheme: digits, leading digits, spaces, tabs, CR, LF, other control bytes, '+', '-', '.', '/', '\\', ':', '~', '[', '{', DEL (0x7F), and bytes >= 0x80. No RFC 3986 ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "-" / "." ) check is performed, and there is no fallback-to-path when the scheme looks illegal.

An EMPTY scheme is legal and distinct from 'no scheme'. If the string begins with "://", scheme is the empty string but the authority parse still runs on the remainder — host/port are populated. Contrast with the no-separator case where the whole string lands in path.
rules.evidence: '://b' -> ['' | b | -1 | '' | '']. '://a.com:8080/p?q' -> ['' | 'a.com' | 8080 | '/p' | 'q'] (empty scheme, yet host and port fully parsed). '://http://a' -> ['' | http | -1 | '//a' | '']. Compare 'a.com' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a.com' | ''] where the same empty scheme line is printed but nothing is treated as authority.

rules.rule: Because the separator is matched greedily-left as the literal "://", a scheme may END in ':'. Extra colons before the '//' are absorbed into the scheme, and the scheme may itself contain ':'.
rules.evidence: 'a:b://c' -> ['a:b' | c | -1 | '' | ''] (this alone disproves any 'find first colon, then require //' implementation, which would have yielded no scheme). 'a:://b' -> ['a:' | b | -1 | '' | '']. ':://a' -> [':' | a | -1 | '' | '']. '::://a' -> ['::' | a | -1 | '' | ''].

rules.rule: The scheme IS case-normalized to lowercase; the mapping is exactly ASCII A-Z -> a-z. Bytes adjacent to A-Z in ASCII ('@', '[', '\\', ']', '^', '_', '`', '{', '|', '}') and all bytes >= 0x80 are left byte-identical (no locale/UTF-8 awareness).
rules.evidence: 'HTTP://a.com' -> [http | a.com]. 'HtTp://A.CoM' -> [http | A.CoM]. 'HTTP+X://a' -> ['http+x' | a]. 'A B C://d' -> ['a b c' | d]. '@AZ`az://b' -> ['@az`az' | b] (only A and Z changed). 'Z[A://b' -> ['z[a' | b]. '~ZA~://b' -> ['~za~' | b]. '[\]^_`{|}://a' -> unchanged '[\]^_`{|}'. 'A\xC0B://h' -> ['a\xC0b' | h] (0xC0 NOT folded to 0xE0). 'ÄÖÜ://a' (UTF-8 C3 84 C3 96 C3 9C) -> scheme bytes unchanged.

rules.rule: The HOST is NOT lowercased, and neither are path or query. Only the scheme is case-folded.
rules.evidence: 'HtTp://A.CoM' -> [http | 'A.CoM' | -1 | '' | '']. 'HTTP://A.COM/PaTh?QuErY=V' -> [http | 'A.COM' | -1 | '/PaTh' | 'QuErY=V']. 'a://B.C/D?E#F' -> [a | 'B.C' | -1 | '/D' | 'E']. 'AB://\xC0\xDF' -> ['ab' | '\xC0\xDF'].

rules.rule: Order of operations: (1) everything from the FIRST '#' to end of string is discarded outright; (2) the remaining text is split at the first '?' into pre-query and query; (3) the "://" search happens only within the pre-query part. Consequently a '#' or a '?' appearing before a "://" destroys the scheme entirely.
rules.evidence: Fragment-before-scheme: 'a#b://c' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | ''] (had the '#' not been stripped first, scheme would be 'a#b'). '#a://b' -> all empty, path ''. 'a#://b' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | '']. Query-before-scheme: 'a?b://c' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | 'b://c'] (scheme would have been 'a?b' otherwise). 'x?y://z' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'x' | 'y://z']. '?a://b' -> ['' | '' | -1 | '' | 'a://b']. '?://a' -> ['' | '' | -1 | '' | '://a']. 'a?://b' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | '://b']. '#' precedes '?': 'a#b?c://d' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | ''] — query is EMPTY, so the '#' cut ran before the '?' split (a '?'-first implementation would have given query 'c://d'). Confirmed again by 'http://a.com/p#frag?q=1' -> [http | a.com | -1 | '/p' | ''].

rules.rule: Only 2 slashes are consumed as part of the separator; any additional slashes fall through into the remainder, producing an EMPTY host and a path that keeps the surplus slashes.
A "://" at the very end of the string yields the scheme plus an empty host, port -1, empty path, empty query. Nothing after the separator is required.
No scheme is special-cased: there is no default-port table and no scheme-specific parsing branch. Every recognized scheme with no explicit port prints port -1, including http/https/ftp/file/ws.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com' -> port -1. 'https://a.com' -> port -1. 'ftp://a.com' -> port -1. 'ws://a' -> [ws | a | -1]. 'gopher://a' -> [gopher | a | -1]. 'file:///etc/passwd' -> [file | '' | -1 | '/etc/passwd' | '']. Explicit ports are echoed verbatim: 'http://a.com:80' -> port 80; 'https://a.com:443' -> port 443.

rules.rule: There is no whitespace trimming anywhere around the scheme — leading/interior/trailing spaces are preserved inside the scheme string (after ASCII lowercasing).

rules.rule: No length limit on the scheme, and parsing never fails: every input tested (including '', ':', '//', '///', '#', '?', a 500-byte scheme, and raw non-UTF-8 bytes) produced exactly 5 lines and exit status 0. The only nonzero exit is the driver's own argc<2 guard (exit 1).

```cpp
        query_ = rest.substr(qp + 1, npos);        // -> +0x28
        rest   = rest.substr(0, qp);
    }

    // --- (3) SCHEME via "://": 40435e ---
    size_t sp = rest.find("://", 0);               // find(const char*, 0)
    if (sp != npos) {
        scheme_ = to_lower(rest.substr(0, sp));    // -> +0x00, lowercased
        rest    = rest.substr(sp + 3, npos);       // +3 == strlen("://")

        // --- (4) AUTHORITY / PATH split at first '/': 40442a ---
        size_t slash = rest.find('/', 0);
        std::string authority;                     // local slot -0xb0
        if (slash != npos) {
            authority = rest.substr(0, slash);
            path_     = rest.substr(slash, npos);  // -> +0x20, KEEPS the leading '/'
        } else {
            authority = rest;                      // copy-assign; path_ stays EMPTY
        }

        // --- (5) USERINFO via '@' inside authority: 404501 ---
        size_t at = authority.find('@', 0);
        if (at != npos) {
            userinfo_ = authority.substr(0, at);        // -> +0x08
            authority = authority.substr(at + 1, npos);
        }

        // --- (6) PORT via ':' inside authority: 4045b2 ---
        size_t colon = authority.find(':', 0);
        if (colon != npos) {
            host_ = authority.substr(0, colon);         // -> +0x10
            try {
                port_ = std::stoi(authority.substr(colon + 1, npos),
                                  /*pos=*/nullptr, /*base=*/10);   // esi=0, edx=0xa
                if (port_ < 0 || port_ > 65535)         // js / cmp $0xffff; jg
                    port_ = -1;
            } catch (...) {                             // 404847: __cxa_begin_catch
                port_ = -1;                             // 404856
            }                                           // 40485d: __cxa_end_catch
        } else {
            host_ = authority;                          // copy-assign
        }
    } else {
        // no "://" anywhere -> everything left is the path
        path_ = rest;                                   // 4046d5, copy-assign into +0x20
    }

    // --- (7) validity: 4046f2 ---
    valid_ = !host_.empty() || !path_.empty();
    return valid_;                                      // movzbl +0x38 -> ebx -> eax
}
```

### Behavioural consequences that fall straight out of this control flow
- **Order matters:** `'#'` is stripped before `'?'`, and both before `"://"`. So a `#` or `?` appearing inside the userinfo/host/port region is *not* treated as part of the authority — `http://a:8#0/x` would give `fragment_="0/x"` and `port_` from `stoi("8")`.
- **Scheme detection requires the literal `"://"`.** `mailto:x@y` has no `"://"`, so the *entire* string lands in `path_` and `scheme_`/`host_` stay empty. Protocol-relative `//host/p` also becomes pure path.
- **Only the first `/` after `"://"` splits authority from path.** If there is no `/`, `path_` is left **empty** (not `"/"`) — asymmetric with `set_path()`, which force-prepends `"/"`.
- **`'@'` search is on the authority substring only** (post-path-split), so a `@` in the path can't be mistaken for userinfo. But it is `find` (first `@`), not `rfind` — a `@` inside a password breaks the split.
- **`':'` search is likewise first-occurrence on the authority**, with no `[...]` bracket handling → a bare IPv6 literal `http://[::1]:80/` mis-splits (`host_="["`, `stoi(":1]:80")` throws → `port_ = -1`). `is_host_valid` does allow `[`, `]`, `:` — but it is never called.
- **`std::stoi` semantics leak through:** `"80abc"` parses as `80` (trailing garbage silently ignored); `""`/`"abc"` throws `invalid_argument` → caught → `-1`; `"99999999999"` throws `out_of_range` → `-1`; `"+80"`/`" 80"` are accepted by `strtol`; `"-1"` parses to `-1` and then hits the `port_ < 0` clamp (also `-1`).
- **`valid_` is extremely permissive:** any non-empty input reaches `valid_ == true` via the no-scheme `path_ = rest` branch. `parse("")` is the only false case. `valid_` is never refreshed by any setter, so it goes stale after `set_host("")`.
- `parse()`'s `to_lower` applies to the scheme **only**; the host keeps its original case unless `normalize_case()` is called.

### Related parsers, for completeness
- `parse_query_params() const` (`4050a8`) — memoized on `+0x70`; loops over `query_`, `find('&', pos)` (`$0x26` @`405107`), then `find('=', 0)` (`$0x3d` @`405164`) on each token; `key = url_decode(tok.substr(0, eq))`, `value = url_decode(tok.substr(eq+1, npos))`, stored via `map::operator[]`; a token with no `=` maps to `""` (`40d0bd`). Mutates through `const` → members are `mutable`.
- `normalize_path()` (`4059d2`) — splits `path_` with `istringstream` + `getline(..., '/')`, compares each segment against `".."` (pop_back) and `"."` (skip), rejoins with `"/"` into an `ostringstream`, preserving a leading `/` if `path_[0]=='/'` (`cmp $0x2f` @`405b73`).
- `to_string()` (`404d14`) is the exact inverse of `parse`: `scheme_ + "://"` (if scheme non-empty), `userinfo_ + "@"`, `host_`, `":" + to_string(port_)` (if `port_ != -1`), `path_`, `"?" + query_`, `"#" + fragment_`.

uncertainties: std::stoi-with-try/catch vs strtol/strtoll-with-endptr-check vs istringstream>>int are behaviorally INDISTINGUISHABLE through this interface. Every value that would make std::stoi throw std::out_of_range (magnitude > INT_MAX) is also > 65535 and therefore hits the same -1 sentinel as the explicit range check; and std::invalid_argument also maps to -1. I designed and ran the only discriminators that exist (4294967296 -> -1 rules out int truncation; 'x' -> -1 rules out bare atoi; ' 8'/'+8' -> 8 rule out from_chars and a digit-only loop; '8x' -> 8 rules out a whole-string-consumed check), so a Rust port can pick any of them as long as it reproduces: strtol-style prefix scan (isspace skip, one optional sign, base-10 digits, stop at first non-digit), require >=1 digit, then accept only 0..65535 else -1.

Whether -1 is stored as a genuine sentinel int or as an Option is unobservable: 'http://a', 'http://a:', 'http://a:x', 'http://a:-1', 'http://a:65536' all print exactly '-1' with identical other four fields. A Rust port that models port as Option<u16> must print -1 for None AND for every invalid/out-of-range case, which is equivalent.

Whether the isspace() set used is locale-dependent could not be fully probed: LC_ALL=C/en_US.UTF-8/de_DE.UTF-8 all gave identical results for the digit cases, but I did not find a locale where an extra character is whitespace. Bytes 0x80/0xff/0xa0/0xc2 in the port position were fuzzed (400 random cases) and never produced a parsed number, only -1, under the default locale.

Embedded NUL bytes in the port component are untestable through argv (the C string is truncated at the NUL): 'http://a:\x008' behaves as 'http://a:' -> -1 and 'http://a:8\x000' behaves as 'http://a:8' -> 8. So NUL-specific behavior inside the port is unknown/unreachable via this driver.

Port strings around 1 MB could not be tested: exec fails with E2BIG ('Argument list too long', shell exit 126) before the program runs. Verified up to 100000 digits, which is exit=0 / port '-1' / empty stderr.

The exact form of the range predicate (v >= 0 && v <= 65535 vs v >= 0 && v < 65536 vs unsigned compare after sign handling) is not distinguishable, but all candidates agree on every probe including the negative-zero case ('-0' -> 0).

result.dimension: PORT parsing — how the port substring is located within the URL and how it is converted to the int returned by port()

rules.rule: No input crashes, aborts, or lets an exception escape. Across ~200 probes (including a 100000-digit port, a 100000-zero port, 5000 leading spaces, and all 256 possible single leading bytes) the program always exited 0, wrote nothing to stderr, and printed exactly 5 newline-terminated lines.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:' + 100000 '9' chars -> exit=0, stderr empty, lines: http / a.com / -1 / '' / ''. Byte-scan of 'http://a.com:<BYTE>80' for BYTE=1..255 -> every case exit=0, sig=0, stderr empty.

rules.rule: A port is only ever looked for inside an authority, and an authority only exists when the URL contains '//' immediately after the scheme's ':'. With no '://' the whole string becomes the path and port is -1.
The authority ends at the first '/', '?', or '#' after the '//'. A ':' at or after that point is never treated as a port separator.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com/p:80' -> http/a.com/-1//p:80/''. 'http://a.com?x=:80' -> http/a.com/-1/''/x=:80. 'http://a.com#f:80' -> http/a.com/-1/''/''. Contrast 'http://a.com:80/:90' -> http/a.com/80//:90/'' and 'http://a.com:8080/p/:9090' -> 8080 with path /p/:9090.

rules.rule: Userinfo is stripped from the authority BEFORE the port colon is located, and the split is at the FIRST '@' in the authority (not the last). So a ':' that lies inside the userinfo is never read as a port.
rules.evidence: 'http://user:80@a.com' -> http/a.com/-1/''/'' (the '80' is NOT taken as a port). 'http://u:1@v:2@a.com:3' -> http/v/2/''/'' — first-'@' stripping leaves 'v:2@a.com:3', giving host 'v' and port-string '2@a.com:3' -> 2. Last-'@' stripping would have given host a.com and port 3. Also 'http://u@a.com:80@b.com:90' -> http/a.com/80/''/'' and 'http://a.com:80@b.com:90/p' -> http/b.com/90//p/''.

rules.rule: Inside the remaining host-part, the port string is taken from immediately after the FIRST ':' (later colons are not special to the splitter). Host is everything before that first colon.
rules.evidence: 'http://[::1]:8080' -> http/'['/-1/''/'' — host is the single char '[', proving the split is at the first ':' and the port-string was '::1]:8080' (unparseable). 'https://[2001:db8::1]:443' -> https/'[2001'/-1/''/''. 'http://a.com::8080' -> http/a.com/-1/''/''. 'http://a.com:8080:9090' -> http/a.com/8080/''/''. 'http://a.com:80:' -> 80.

rules.rule: Conversion is a std::stoi-style base-10 PREFIX parse of the port string, not a full-string validation: optional run of leading whitespace, then an optional single '+' or '-', then ASCII decimal digits; parsing stops at the first non-digit and all trailing bytes are silently ignored.
rules.evidence: Trailing junk ignored: 'http://a.com:80abc' -> 80; 'http://a.com:0080abc' -> 80; 'http://a.com:80.5' -> 80; 'http://a.com:1e3' -> 1; 'http://a.com:8 0' -> 8; 'http://a.com:8_0' -> 8; 'http://a.com:1;2' -> 1; 'http://a.com:80%20' -> 80; 'http://a.com:80 ' -> 80. Leading whitespace accepted: 'http://a.com: 80' -> 80; 'http://a.com:  80' -> 80; 'http://a.com:\t80' -> 80. Leading sign accepted: 'http://a.com:+80' -> 80; 'http://a.com: +80' -> 80; 'http://a.com:-0' -> 0. Order enforced (space cannot follow sign): 'http://a.com:+ 80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:- 80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:++80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:-+80' -> -1. No leading digit at all -> -1: 'http://a.com:abc' -> -1; 'http://a.com:abc80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:.80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:%2280' -> -1.

rules.rule: The radix is fixed at 10. Leading zeros are NOT octal and '0x'/'0X' is NOT hex — the parse just consumes decimal digits.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:080' -> 80 (octal would be 64); 'http://a.com:0777' -> 777 (octal would be 511); 'http://a.com:00080' -> 80; 'http://a.com:0x50' -> 0 (hex would be 80); 'http://a.com:0X50' -> 0; 'http://a.com:0b11' -> 0.

rules.rule: The accepted leading-whitespace set is exactly C-locale isspace: 0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF, 0x0D CR, 0x20 SPACE. Every other non-digit, non-'+' leading byte yields -1.
rules.evidence: Exhaustive byte scan of 'http://a.com:<BYTE>80' for BYTE=1..255: the only bytes producing a non-(-1) port were 9,10,11,12,13,32 (all -> 80), 43 '+' (-> 80), and 48-57 (digits, '0'->80, '1'->180, ... '9'->980). Byte 45 '-' produced -1. Byte 0xFF produced -1.

rules.rule: Only ASCII digits count; no Unicode digit forms are recognized.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:٨٠' (UTF-8 bytes d9 a8 d9 a0, Arabic-Indic 80) -> http/a.com/-1/''/''. 'http://a.com:１２３' (fullwidth 123) -> http/a.com/-1/''/''.

rules.rule: After conversion there is an explicit range check: the value is accepted only if 0 <= v <= 65535; anything else returns -1. There is NO clamping, NO wrapping, and NO 16-bit truncation.
rules.evidence: Boundary: 'http://a.com:65535' -> 65535, 'http://a.com:65534' -> 65534, 'http://a.com:+65535' -> 65535, 'http://a.com:00065535' -> 65535; 'http://a.com:65536' -> -1, 'http://a.com:00065536' -> -1, 'http://a.com:+65536' -> -1, 'http://a.com:655360' -> -1, 'http://a.com:99999' -> -1. Zero accepted: 'http://a.com:0' -> 0, 'http://a.com:+0' -> 0, 'http://a.com:-0' -> 0, 'http://a.com:  +0  ' -> 0, 100000 zeros -> 0. Negatives rejected: 'http://a.com:-1' -> -1, 'http://a.com:-80' -> -1, 'http://a.com:-65535' -> -1. Rules out uint16_t storage (65536 would print 0). Rules out a bare (int) cast of a long strtol result with no range check: 'http://a.com:4294967296' -> -1, not 0. Rules out any clamping: 'http://a.com:2147483647x' -> -1, not 65535 and not 2147483647.

rules.rule: An out-of-int-range numeric prefix is caught and also yields -1 (i.e. the throwing/erroring conversion is wrapped, and its failure is mapped to the same sentinel).
The conversion is NOT atoi/strtol-without-failure-detection: a 'no conversion performed' condition is detected and distinguished from a parsed 0.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:abc' -> -1, whereas atoi("abc") == 0 would have printed 0. Compare 'http://a.com:0x50' -> 0 (a real parsed zero). Likewise 'http://a.com:' (empty) -> -1 and 'http://a.com: ' (whitespace only) -> -1.

rules.rule: -1 is a single overloaded sentinel meaning 'no usable port'. It is emitted for all of: no ':' in the authority, an empty port string, a whitespace-only port string, a port string with no leading digits, and a numerically out-of-range port. These cases are NOT distinguishable from port() alone. Because the valid range is 0..65535, -1 can never be a genuine port value.
rules.evidence: no colon: 'http://a.com' -> -1. empty: 'http://a.com:' -> -1 and 'http://a.com:/p' -> http/a.com/-1//p/''. whitespace-only: 'http://a.com: ' -> -1. non-numeric: 'http://a.com:abc' -> -1. out of range: 'http://a.com:65536' -> -1. negative: 'http://a.com:-80' -> -1.

rules.rule: An invalid or out-of-range port does not abort or poison the rest of the parse: the host is still truncated at the colon, and path/query are still extracted normally.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:abc/p?q=1' -> http/a.com/-1//p/q=1. 'http://a.com:99999/p?q=1#f' -> http/a.com/-1//p/q=1. 'http://a.com:65536/p' -> http/a.com/-1//p/''. 'http://a.com:-1/p' -> http/a.com/-1//p/''.

rules.rule: There is no length limit or sanity cap on the port string; the numeric value alone decides. Arbitrarily long leading-zero runs parse fine.
An empty host does not prevent port parsing; the port colon can be the very first character of the authority.
Spaces inside the authority do not terminate it, so a space between host and ':' still yields a parsed port (with the space kept in host).
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com :80' -> http/'a.com '/80/''/''. Also ' http://a.com:80' -> ' http'/a.com/80/''/'' — no trimming of the input at all.

rules.rule: A NUL byte in argv simply truncates the URL at the C-string level before the library sees it; this is not port logic.
rules.evidence: argv 'http://a.com:80\x0090' -> http/a.com/80/''/'' (behaves as 'http://a.com:80'). argv 'http://a.com:\x0080' -> http/a.com/-1/''/'' (behaves as 'http://a.com:').

rules.rule: For every valid in-range numeric port the returned value equals the decimal value exactly (identity mapping, no off-by-one, no reserved-port special-casing).

uncertainties: Whether the port substring handed to the converter is 'everything after the first colon to the end of the host-part' or 'the text between the first and second colon'. These two hypotheses are observationally EQUIVALENT for every probe I could design, because ':' is never a digit and therefore always terminates the prefix parse at exactly the same place. Discriminating probes attempted and found non-discriminating: 'http://a.com:8080:9090' (8080 either way), 'http://a.com:65536:80' / 'http://a.com: :80' / 'http://a.com:+:80' (-1 either way), 'http://a.com:/80' (-1 either way). The 'host = text before first colon' half IS nailed down by 'http://[::1]:8080' -> host '['.

Whether the converter is std::stoi wrapped in try/catch, or strtol/strtoul with an endptr!=start and ERANGE check. Both explain 100% of the data. Definitively RULED OUT: (a) atoi / no-failure-detection, since 'http://a.com:abc' -> -1 not 0; (b) std::from_chars or a hand-rolled isdigit loop, since ' 80' and '+80' both parse; (c) storage in uint16_t, since ':65536' -> -1 not 0; (d) an unchecked (int) narrowing of a long result, since ':4294967296' -> -1 not 0.

Whether the range test is signed ('v < 0 || v > 65535' on an int) or unsigned ('v > 65535' after an unsigned parse). ':-0' -> 0 proves the '-' character is consumed by the converter rather than rejected as a bad char, but every other negative magnitude (-1, -80, -65535, -2147483648) yields -1 under either formulation. A signed int parse plus a two-sided range check is the simplest fit and matches the -1 sentinel being an int.

Whether the -1 for 'no colon present' and the -1 for 'colon present but unparseable/out-of-range' come from the same code path or from two different assignments. port() alone cannot distinguish them; no other printed field changes (host is truncated at the colon in both the valid and invalid cases, e.g. 'http://a.com:abc' -> host 'a.com').

Whether leading-whitespace skipping and '+' acceptance are deliberate or merely inherited defaults of the underlying conversion function. Behaviorally they are present; intent is unknowable black-box.

Behavior under a non-C locale was not exercised (the process ran with the default environment). If the implementation uses a locale-sensitive conversion, digit/whitespace classification could in principle differ elsewhere.
Whether port() is recomputed per call or cached at construction — the driver calls it once, so this is unobservable.

========================================================================
REFERENCE SPEC: url_parser::URL::parse  (verified byte-for-byte against
/workspace/dataset/test5_executable, GCC 12 -O0, pre-C++11 std::string ABI)
========================================================================

--- 0. DRIVER (test5.cpp) -----------------------------------------------
main(argc, argv):
    if argc < 2: exit(1)                  # NO output at all, not even newlines
    u = URL(argv[1])                       # ctor resets state then calls parse()
    write(scheme_bytes); write("\n")
    write(host_bytes);   write("\n")
    write(decimal_int(port)); write("\n")  # plain ostream<<int: "-1", "0", "65535";
                                           # no '+', no grouping, no padding, no locale effect
    write(path_bytes);   write("\n")
    write(query_bytes);  write("\n")
    exit(0)

Notes on the I/O contract:
  * Exactly 5 '\n'-terminated records are emitted. Fields are raw bytes,
    echoed verbatim; a field containing 0x0A therefore produces MORE than 5
    physical lines. Empty input yields exactly 7 bytes: 0A 0A 2D 31 0A 0A 0A.
  * argv[1] is a NUL-terminated C string, so an embedded 0x00 truncates the
    input before the parser ever sees it (execve/libc artifact, NOT parser logic).
  * argv[2..] are ignored entirely.
  * Exit status is always 0 whenever argv[1] exists. Nothing is ever written to
    stderr. No input can make the process abort, hang, or throw out of main.
  * The process never calls setlocale(), so it runs in the "C" locale no matter
    what LC_ALL/LC_CTYPE say (verified: LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 still folds 'I'->'i',
    and 0xA0 is never whitespace).

--- 1. PARSE -----------------------------------------------------------
All indices are BYTE indices into a length-counted byte string (std::string):
no NUL sensitivity, no UTF-8 awareness, no character classes beyond the ones
spelled out below.

find_byte(s, b)   := smallest i in [0, len(s)) with s[i] == b, else NONE.
                     (forward search from offset 0 -- NOT rfind, NOT
                      find_first_of; the start offset argument is literally 0
                      at every one of the 5 call sites)
find_sub3(s, "://"):= smallest i in [0, len(s)-2] with s[i..i+3) == ":" "/" "/",
                     else NONE.  (forward search from offset 0)
s[a..b)           := bytes a inclusive .. b exclusive
s[a..]            := s[a..len(s))   (implemented as substr(a, npos))

parse(url):
    # ---- reset (every field, unconditionally) ----
    scheme = ""; userinfo = ""; host = ""; port = -1
    path = "";  query = "";  fragment = ""
    rest = url                       # working copy

    # ---- STEP 1: FRAGMENT. Highest precedence. Runs on the RAW input,
    #              BEFORE query split, BEFORE scheme detection. ----
    hp = find_byte(rest, 0x23 '#')
    if hp != NONE:
        fragment = rest[hp+1 ..]     # stored but NEVER printed by the driver
        rest     = rest[0 .. hp)     # '#' itself is dropped
    # => no byte at or after the first '#' can ever reach scheme/host/port/path/query.
    # => a '#' before a "://" destroys scheme AND host.
    # => only the FIRST '#' matters; later '#'s are already inside the discard.

    # ---- STEP 2: QUERY. Second precedence. Runs on the fragment-stripped
    #              string, over its WHOLE length, BEFORE scheme detection. ----
    qp = find_byte(rest, 0x3F '?')
    if qp != NONE:
        query = rest[qp+1 ..]        # to end; later '?'s stay inside query
        rest  = rest[0 .. qp)
    # => a '?' after the first '#' produces NO query (it was already discarded).
    # => a '?' before a "://" destroys scheme AND host; the rest of the URL
    #    (including further "://", '@', ':', '/') lands in query UNPARSED.
    # => empty query and absent query are indistinguishable in the 5-line output.

    # ---- STEP 3: SCHEME, keyed on the literal 3-byte sequence "://" ----
    sp = find_sub3(rest, "://")
    if sp == NONE:
        # ***** NO-AUTHORITY BRANCH *****
        path = rest                  # the ENTIRE remainder, verbatim
        # scheme stays "", host stays "", port stays -1
        return                       # nothing else is parsed: ':' '/' '@' inert
    scheme = ascii_lower(rest[0 .. sp))   # may be EMPTY and that is legal
    rest   = rest[sp+3 ..]                # exactly +3 -- only 2 slashes consumed,
                                          # surplus slashes fall through to path
    # ascii_lower is: for each byte b (taken as unsigned char), C-locale tolower.
    # Verified by exhaustive 1..255 sweep: EXACTLY 0x41..0x5A ('A'..'Z') map to
    # 0x61..0x7A ('a'..'z'); every other byte, including 0x40 '@', 0x5B '[',
    # 0x5C '\', 0x60 '`', 0x7B '{', 0x7F, and ALL bytes 0x80..0xFF, is identity.
    # There is NO scheme character-set validation and NO length limit: '/', ':',
    # '@', ' ', TAB, CR, control bytes, digits, punctuation, high bytes all pass.
    # Only the FIRST "://" is the separator; later ones are ordinary bytes.

    # ---- STEP 4: AUTHORITY / PATH split at the FIRST '/' ----
    slash = find_byte(rest, 0x2F '/')
    if slash != NONE:
        authority = rest[0 .. slash)
        path      = rest[slash ..]   # INCLUDES the leading '/'; runs to end of rest
    else:
        authority = rest
        path      = ""               # NO synthesized "/" -- path stays empty
    # '?' and '#' were already removed, so '/' is the ONLY authority terminator.
    # Backslash, ';', ',', space, TAB, CR, NUL-free control bytes, high bytes,
    # '%' escapes: none of them terminate the authority.

    # ---- STEP 5: USERINFO strip at the FIRST '@' of the authority ----
    at = find_byte(authority, 0x40 '@')
    if at != NONE:
        userinfo  = authority[0 .. at)   # stored, never printed
        authority = authority[at+1 ..]   # remainder is NOT re-scanned for '@'
    # FIRST '@', not last (non-RFC): "u@v@w" leaves authority "v@w".
    # Confined to the authority, so an '@' in path or query is an ordinary byte.
    # Runs BEFORE the port colon, so a ':' left of the first '@' is userinfo.

    # ---- STEP 6: HOST / PORT split at the FIRST ':' of what remains ----
    colon = find_byte(authority, 0x3A ':')
    if colon == NONE:
        host = authority             # port stays -1
        return
    host     = authority[0 .. colon) # FIRST ':', not last; no '[' ']' IPv6 logic
    port_str = authority[colon+1 ..] # to END of authority (may contain ':', '@', ...)
    port     = convert_port(port_str)
    if port < 0 or port > 65535:     # signed compare against 65535
        port = -1
    return

--- 2. convert_port: exact semantics -----------------------------------
The binary calls std::stoi(port_str, /*pos=*/nullptr, /*base=*/10), which is
__gnu_cxx::__stoa(&strtol, "stoi", ...), wrapped in a try/catch whose LSDA
action filter resolves to a NULL ttype, i.e. a bare `catch (...)` whose body is
exactly `port_ = -1;`. Both std::invalid_argument and std::out_of_range are
thrown in practice and both are swallowed silently (exit 0, empty stderr).

convert_port(s) -> int:
    i = 0
    # (a) skip a run of leading whitespace. The set is EXACTLY C-locale isspace:
    #     {0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF, 0x0D CR, 0x20 SPACE}.
    #     Verified by exhaustive byte scan; 0xA0 and every other byte are NOT ws.
    while i < len(s) and s[i] in {0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20}: i += 1
    # (b) at most ONE optional sign, immediately after the whitespace run
    neg = false
    if i < len(s) and (s[i]=='+' or s[i]=='-'):
        neg = (s[i]=='-'); i += 1
    # (c) at least one ASCII digit 0x30..0x39 must follow IMMEDIATELY.
    #     No whitespace may follow the sign. Only ASCII digits count -- no
    #     Unicode/fullwidth/Arabic-Indic digits. Base is fixed 10: no octal
    #     interpretation of leading zeros, no 0x/0X/0b prefixes.
    if i >= len(s) or not (0x30 <= s[i] <= 0x39):
        return SENTINEL_FAIL                 # -> invalid_argument -> caught -> -1
    # (d) consume the maximal run of ASCII digits; STOP at the first non-digit
    #     and silently IGNORE every remaining byte (prefix parse, no
    #     whole-string-consumed check).
    mag = 0 (arbitrary precision)
    while i < len(s) and 0x30 <= s[i] <= 0x39:
        mag = mag*10 + (s[i]-0x30); i += 1
    v = neg ? -mag : +mag
    # (e) strtol overflow: if v does not fit in i64 -> ERANGE -> out_of_range -> -1
    if v < -2^63 or v > 2^63-1: return SENTINEL_FAIL
    # (f) long->int narrowing check: if v does not fit in i32 -> out_of_range -> -1
    if v < -2^31 or v > 2^31-1:  return SENTINEL_FAIL
    return v as i32
    # SENTINEL_FAIL is caught and mapped to -1 by the caller.

Simplification that is observationally IDENTICAL (recommended for a port):
    parse the prefix as above into an arbitrary-precision signed integer;
    if no digit was consumed -> -1;
    else if value is in 0..=65535 -> value;
    else -> -1.
Because every value that would throw (|v| > INT_MAX) is also outside 0..65535,
and because the explicit range check runs after the conversion, all failure
modes collapse onto the single sentinel -1.

CRITICAL corner: "-0" (and " -0", "-00") parses to 0, passes the >=0 check, and
yields port 0. A naive "reject if the string starts with '-'" shortcut is WRONG.
"-1" yields -1 only because the range check rejects it -- it is indistinguishable
from the absent-port sentinel.

--- 3. THINGS THAT DO NOT HAPPEN (all verified in the binary) ----------
  * No default/implicit port for ANY scheme. There is no "http"/"https" string
    literal anywhere in the binary and no scheme->port table; 65535 is the only
    port-related numeric constant. Every schemeless-port URL prints -1.
  * No percent-decoding anywhere. "%23", "%3F", "%2F", "%40", "%3A", "%20",
    lone "%", malformed "%zz" all pass through literally and never act as
    delimiters.
  * No whitespace trimming. A trim() function exists in the binary but is never
    called from any code path.
  * No path normalization. normalize()/normalize_case()/normalize_path()/
    normalize_query() exist but the constructor never calls them: ".", "..",
    empty segments and duplicate slashes are preserved byte-for-byte.
  * No validation. is_scheme_valid(), is_host_valid(), is_port_valid() and
    split_path() exist but are never called. Parsing never fails.
  * No host lowercasing, no IDN/punycode processing, no UTF-8 validation.
    Only the scheme is case-folded.
  * No IPv6 bracket handling: '[' and ']' are ordinary host bytes.
  * No length limits: schemes/hosts/paths/queries/port strings of 100k+ bytes
    round-trip exactly (only the kernel MAX_ARG_STRLEN ~131072 stops argv).
  * The authority-end scan is find('/'), not find_first_of("/?#") -- behaviorally
    indistinguishable here because '?' and '#' were already removed.
rules: OUTPUT SHAPE: with argv[1] present, exactly 5 '\n'-terminated records are written to stdout in the order scheme, host, port, path, query; exit status is 0 and stderr is always empty. With argc<2 the driver writes nothing at all and exits 1.
Fields are raw byte strings echoed verbatim, so a field containing 0x0A yields more than 5 physical lines (e.g. 'http://a<LF>b.com' prints 6 lines).

port() is printed by plain ostream<<int: '-1' for the sentinel, '0'..'65535' otherwise; never a '+', never thousands grouping, never padding. Locale has no effect (the program never calls setlocale, so it stays in the C locale even under LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8).

PRECEDENCE (absolute, never revisited): (1) truncate at first '#'; (2) split query at first '?'; (3) find first "://"; (4) split authority/path at first '/'; (5) strip through first '@' in authority; (6) split host/port at first ':' in authority.

STEP 1 fragment: everything from the FIRST 0x23 '#' to end of the RAW input is discarded before any other parsing. No byte at or after that '#' can appear in any of the 5 fields. Only the first '#' matters.
A '#' occurring before a "://" destroys scheme AND host: 'ht#tp://a.com' -> ''/''/-1/'ht'/''.
STEP 2 query: query = everything after the FIRST 0x3F '?' of the fragment-stripped string, to its end. The search spans the whole string, not just the path region.
Because '#' is cut first, a '?' that appears after the first '#' produces NO query. Discriminator: 'a.com#f?q=1' -> query '' (not 'q=1').
Only the first '?' is a delimiter; later '?' bytes are ordinary query content ('http://a.com/p?a=1?b=2' -> query 'a=1?b=2').
A '?' before a "://" destroys scheme AND host; the remainder lands in query completely unparsed, including further "://", '@', ':' and '/'.
Empty query and absent query are indistinguishable (both print an empty line 5). Same for empty vs absent fragment.

STEP 3 scheme: the one and only trigger for authority parsing is the literal 3-byte sequence 0x3A 0x2F 0x2F "://". A bare ':' is insufficient; '//' without a preceding ':' is insufficient; ':' and '//' must be contiguous.
If "://" is absent from the fragment- and query-stripped remainder, scheme='', host='', port=-1 and the ENTIRE remainder becomes the path verbatim. In that branch ':', '/', '@' are completely inert.
scheme = the bytes strictly before the FIRST "://", ASCII-lowercased. Later "://" occurrences are never the separator.

There is NO scheme character-set validation and no length limit: digits, leading digits, spaces, TAB, CR, control bytes, '/', '\\', ':', '@', '+', '-', '.', '~', '[', '{', DEL and bytes >=0x80 are all accepted as scheme bytes.
A scheme may end in ':' and may contain ':' ('a:b://c' -> scheme 'a:b'; 'a:://b' -> scheme 'a:'; ':://a' -> scheme ':').

An EMPTY scheme is legal and distinct from 'no scheme': a leading "://" still runs the authority parse ('://a.com:8080/p?q' -> ''/'a.com'/8080/'/p'/'q'), whereas a string with no "://" puts everything in path.

Case folding is EXACTLY bytes 0x41..0x5A -> 0x61..0x7A, applied only to the scheme. Verified by exhaustive 1..255 byte sweep: 0x40 '@', 0x5B '[', 0x5C '\\', 0x60 '`', 0x7B '{', 0x7F and every byte 0x80..0xFF are left identical. Implementation is C-locale tolower on unsigned char.
Host, path and query preserve case and bytes exactly; they are never lowercased, decoded, normalized or trimmed.

The remainder-parse resumes at exactly (index of first "://") + 3. Only two slashes are consumed, so surplus slashes fall into the path with an empty host ('http:///a' -> host '', path '/a'; 'a://///b' -> host '', path '///b').

STEP 4 authority/path: the authority ends at the FIRST 0x2F '/' after the separator; path = that '/' through the end of the (fragment/query-stripped) string, leading '/' INCLUDED. If no '/' exists the path is EMPTY -- no default '/' is synthesized.

Exactly two bytes can terminate a path, and both do so in earlier steps: '?' and '#'. A byte sweep of 1..126 inside a path showed every other byte -- including ':', '@', '\\', ';', '%', '+', '&', '=', space, TAB, CR, DEL -- is retained verbatim.

STEP 5 userinfo: if the authority contains 0x40 '@', everything up to and including the FIRST '@' is discarded. It is find('@'), not rfind('@'), and the remainder is not re-scanned: 'http://a@b@c' -> host 'b@c'.
The '@' search is confined to the authority (before the first '/', and '?'/'#' are already gone), so an '@' in path or query never triggers userinfo stripping.

Userinfo stripping runs BEFORE the port colon is located, so a ':' left of the first '@' is never a port ('http://user:80@a.com' -> port -1) and the port comes from the post-'@' text ('http://a.com:80@b.com:90' -> host 'b.com', port 90).

STEP 6 host/port: host = authority bytes before the FIRST 0x3A ':'; port string = everything after that ':' to the end of the authority. It is find(':'), not rfind(':'): 'http://a.com:80:90' -> host 'a.com', port 80.
No IPv6 bracket handling whatsoever: 'http://[::1]:8080' -> host '[', port -1. '[' and ']' are ordinary bytes ('http://[a]:80' -> host '[a]', port 80).
An empty host is fine and is not an error: 'http://' , 'http://:' , 'http://@' , 'http://a.com@' , 'http://:8080' all parse with host ''.

PORT CONVERSION is a std::stoi/strtol-style base-10 PREFIX parse: optional run of C-locale whitespace {0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20}, then at most ONE '+' or '-', then one or more ASCII digits; parsing stops at the first non-digit and ALL trailing bytes are silently ignored.
Whitespace may precede the sign but NOT follow it: ' +80' -> 80, but '+ 80' -> -1, '- 80' -> -1, '++80' -> -1, '-+80' -> -1, bare '+' or '-' -> -1.

At least one ASCII digit is required; otherwise -1. Only ASCII 0x30..0x39 count -- Arabic-Indic and fullwidth digits are rejected. Radix is fixed 10: '080'->80, '0777'->777, '0x50'->0, '0X50'->0, '0b11'->0.

After conversion an explicit range check accepts only 0 <= v <= 65535; anything else becomes -1. There is NO clamping, NO wraparound, NO uint16 truncation and NO (int) narrowing of a wider result: 65536 -> -1 (not 0), 65616 -> -1 (not 80), 4294967296 -> -1 (not 0), 2147483647 -> -1 (not 65535).
Negative zero is ACCEPTED: '-0', '-00', ' -0' all yield port 0. Every other negative magnitude yields -1. Do not shortcut on a leading '-'.

Out-of-int-range and non-numeric port strings throw std::out_of_range / std::invalid_argument inside std::stoi; a bare catch(...) swallows them and assigns -1. Exit status stays 0 and stderr stays empty (100000-digit ports included).

-1 is a single overloaded sentinel: no ':' in the authority, empty port string, whitespace-only port string, no leading digit, negative value, and out-of-range value are all indistinguishable from port() alone. Since valid ports are 0..65535, -1 is never a genuine port.
A bad port never poisons the other fields: the host is still truncated at the colon and path/query are still extracted ('http://a.com:abc/p?q=1' -> http/a.com/-1//p/q=1).

There are NO default ports for any scheme. 25+ schemes probed (http, https, ftp, file, ws, wss, ssh, ldap, redis, mongodb, ...) all print -1 when no explicit port is given. The binary contains no 'http'/'https' literal and no scheme->port table; 65535 is the only port constant.

No scheme is special-cased at all: 'file:///etc/passwd' -> file/''/-1//etc/passwd/''. No scheme whitelist ('httpx://a.com' parses). Opaque URIs without "://" (mailto:, urn:, tel:, javascript:, data:, about:, 'C:\\path\\file') land wholly in path.
Protocol-relative '//host/path' is NOT supported -- it becomes pure path.
No percent-decoding anywhere: '%23', '%3F', '%2F', '%40', '%3A', '%20', a lone '%' and malformed '%zz' pass through literally and never act as delimiters.
No whitespace trimming anywhere: leading spaces become part of the scheme, interior/trailing spaces stay in host, path and query. (A trim() function exists in the binary but is never called.)
No path normalization: '.', '..', empty segments and duplicate slashes are preserved byte-for-byte. (normalize()/normalize_path() exist but the constructor never calls them.)
No host validation, no IDN/punycode decoding, no UTF-8 validation: empty labels, leading/trailing dots and dashes, 300-char labels, raw 0xFF bytes and UTF-8 sequences all pass through unchanged.

No length limits: 50000-byte schemes, 300-byte hosts, 5000-byte paths, 1200-byte queries, 100000-digit port strings all work with exit 0. The only ceiling is the kernel's MAX_ARG_STRLEN (~131072 bytes) on argv, which is not a parser limit.
Parsing never fails and never throws out of the constructor. Every input tested -- including '', ':', '//', '///', '#', '?', '@', '://' and raw non-UTF-8 bytes -- produced 5 records and exit 0.

An embedded 0x00 in argv truncates the string at the C-string level before the parser runs; this is an execve/libc artifact, not parser behaviour, and internal parsing is length-based (std::string), not NUL-terminated.
Only argv[1] is read; argv[2..] are ignored.

openQuestions: No cross-report conflicts survived verification. I re-ran every discriminating vector in the ten reports against /workspace/dataset/test5_executable and all of them reproduced exactly, including the ones the reports flagged as uncertain (e.g. 'http://u:1@v:2@a.com:3' -> host 'v'/port 2, 'http://a.com:8@0/p' -> host '0', 'x://?@:#' -> query '@:'). The only cross-report differences were in wording, not in observed bytes.

Several reports left as 'observationally equivalent' whether the '#'/'?' handling is (a) truncate-then-split or (b) index-comparison. The binary settles it as (a): parse() literally does rest = rest.substr(0, find('#')) then query = rest.substr(find('?')+1), rest = rest.substr(0, find('?')), all before find("://"). Both models produce identical output, so a reimplementation may use either.

Similarly resolved from the binary: the port string is authority.substr(colon+1) to the END of the authority (not 'between the first and second colon'); and the authority-end scan is find('/'), not find_first_of("/?#"). Both were listed as undecidable black-box, and both choices are behaviorally indistinguishable because '?'/'#' are already gone and ':' always terminates the numeric prefix.

Locale sensitivity is settled and is a non-issue: the program never calls setlocale(), so it runs in the C locale regardless of the environment. Verified LC_ALL=C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8 and tr_TR.UTF-8 all fold 'I'->'i' (not dotless), print '65535' with no grouping, and treat 0xA0 as a non-whitespace, non-digit byte. A Rust port should hardcode ASCII A-Z folding and the six-byte C isspace set.

Embedded NUL bytes inside a field are unreachable through this driver (argv is NUL-terminated), so the parser's behaviour on an interior 0x00 is unobservable here. The implementation is length-based std::string, so a faithful Rust port should treat 0x00 as an ordinary byte; that choice is untestable via argv and only matters if the library is exercised directly.

Empty vs. absent is not distinguishable for query or fragment through these five accessors: 'http://a.com/p', 'http://a.com/p?' and 'http://a.com/p?#f' produce byte-identical output. Internally the binary does store a distinction (a fragment_ field and an unconditional query_ assignment), and fragment() / userinfo() / is_valid() accessors exist, but the driver never prints them, so a port may model query/fragment as either String or Option<String>.

'://' with an empty scheme and an empty authority is indistinguishable from the no-"://" branch whenever path and query are also empty: '', '#', '?', '://', '://#f', '://:' all emit the identical 7 bytes. A reimplementation may take either code path for those specific inputs.

-1 is a single overloaded sentinel: absent colon, empty port text, whitespace-only text, no leading digit, negative value, and out-of-range value are all indistinguishable from port() alone (and from a literal ':-1'). Whether the two -1 assignment sites in the binary are reached is not observable.

Inputs larger than the kernel's MAX_ARG_STRLEN (131072 bytes) cannot be delivered through argv (execve returns E2BIG before the program starts). Verified clean up to 131071 bytes of input and 100000-digit port strings, with no sign of any internal ceiling, but multi-megabyte behaviour is unverified.

The binary contains substantial dead code that the constructor never reaches and that therefore must NOT be replicated: trim(), normalize(), normalize_case(), normalize_path(), normalize_query(), split_path(), is_scheme_valid(), is_host_valid(), is_port_valid(), url_encode(), url_decode(), parse_query_params(), to_string(), and the setters (set_path() force-prepends '/', set_port() clamps). If the differential harness ever calls something other than the five printed accessors, this spec does not cover it.

A byte-position sweep was done for the scheme (all 1..255), the port (all 1..255) and the path (1..126 minus LF), but not exhaustively for the host or query positions. No exotic delimiter was found anywhere and the recovered control flow (five find() calls on fixed bytes plus one find("://")) rules one out, so this is a completeness gap in the evidence rather than a live ambiguity.

result.dimension: Numeric port conversion: boundaries, overflow, signs, whitespace, and non-digit suffixes

rules.rule: NO DIVERGENCE FOUND. After ~72,000 probes targeted at port conversion (exhaustive integer sweep 0..65540, exhaustive single-byte prefix sweep 1..255, exhaustive digit-run-terminator sweep 1..255, 668-case port-string differential fuzz, 2010-case whole-URL differential fuzz), the candidate spec's convert_port() model predicted the binary's port field byte-for-byte in every single case. Both fuzz campaigns reimplemented the spec in Perl and diffed against the binary; both reported divergences=0.
rules.evidence: Differential fuzz results: '/tmp/fuzz.pl' -> 'checked=668 divergences=0'; '/tmp/fuzz2.pl' (all 5 fields compared as raw bytes) -> 'checked=2010 divergences=0'; exhaustive integer sweep -> 'exhaustive 0..65540 checked=65541 divergences=0'.

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: the accept window is exactly 0 <= v <= 65535, inclusive on both ends, with a hard cliff at 65536. Verified exhaustively for every literal decimal integer 0..65540 (65541 runs): each v in 0..65535 printed itself verbatim; 65536..65540 all printed -1. No clamping, no wraparound, no uint16 truncation.
rules.evidence: 'http://h:65535/p' -> http/h/65535//p/'' ; 'http://h:65536/p' -> http/h/-1//p/'' ; exhaustive sweep 0..65540 found 0 mismatches against the predicate (v<=65535 ? v : -1). Also 'http://h:32768' -> 32768 (not a signed-short reject), 'http://h:655350' -> -1 (not 65535).

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: the whitespace-skip set is exactly {0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20}. An exhaustive sweep of all bytes 0x01..0xFF as the single leading byte of the port string found the ONLY bytes yielding port 80 for '<b>80' were 0x09 0x0A 0x0B 0x0C 0x0D 0x20 (whitespace) plus 0x2B '+' (sign) and 0x30 '0' (digit). 0xA0 is NOT whitespace under any locale.
rules.evidence: Sweep output: 'PREFIX byte yields 80: 0x09 0x0A 0x0B 0x0C 0x0D 0x20 0x2B 0x30' and 'PREFIX byte other: 0x31=>180 ... 0x39=>980'. Every other byte gave -1. Confirming singles: 'http://h:\x0D\x0A80/p' -> port 80; 'http://h:\x0B\x0C80/p' -> port 80; 'http://h:\xA080/p' -> port -1; 'http://h:\xC2\xA080/p' -> port -1. Locale-invariant: LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 with '\xA080' still gives -1.

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: whitespace runs of arbitrary length are skipped, and whitespace may PRECEDE the sign but never FOLLOW it. All 36 two-byte whitespace pairs followed by '-0' gave port 0; a 5000-space and a 131000-space run followed by '80' both gave port 80.
CONFIRMED: exactly ONE optional sign. Two sign characters in any combination always yield -1, and a bare sign (with or without leading whitespace) yields -1.

CONFIRMED (the spec's 'CRITICAL corner' is real): negative ZERO is accepted and yields port 0, in any zero-magnitude spelling, with or without leading whitespace, and with arbitrary trailing junk. Every negative NON-zero magnitude yields -1.

CONFIRMED: it is a PREFIX parse with no whole-string-consumed check. The digit run stops at the first non-digit and every remaining byte is silently ignored. An exhaustive sweep of all bytes 0x01..0xFF as the terminator in '80<b>9' returned port 80 for all 254 non-digit bytes (the two exceptions are delimiters handled in earlier parse steps, not conversion behaviour).

Named cases: 'http://h:80abc/p' -> 80 ; 'http://h:65535x' -> 65535 ; 'http://h:80.5/p' -> 80 ; 'http://h:80,90/p' -> 80 ; 'http://h:80:90/p' -> 80 ; 'http://h:1e3/p' -> 1 ; 'http://h:1_0/p' -> 1 ; 'http://h:8\xC2\xB0/p' -> 8 ; 'http://h:80\xA0/p' -> 80 ; 'http://h:65535 65535' -> 65535.

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: at least one ASCII digit 0x30..0x39 must appear immediately after the optional sign; nothing else counts as a digit. Fullwidth (U+FF18), Arabic-Indic (U+0668), Devanagari (U+0968), superscript two (U+00B2), Unicode minus (U+2212) and plus-minus (U+00B1) are all rejected.
rules.evidence: 'http://h:\xEF\xBC\x98\xEF\xBC\x90/p' -> -1 ; 'http://h:\xD9\xA8\xD9\xA0/p' -> -1 ; 'http://h:\xE0\xA5\xA8/p' -> -1 ; 'http://h:\xC2\xB2/p' -> -1 ; 'http://h:\xE2\x88\x9280/p' -> -1 ; 'http://h:\xC2\xB180/p' -> -1 ; 'http://h:abc80/p' -> -1 ; 'http://h:.80' -> -1 ; 'http://h:%2F80' -> -1 (no percent-decoding) ; 'http://h:%2b80' -> -1.

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: radix is fixed 10. Leading zeros are not octal, and 0x/0X/0b/0o prefixes stop the parse after the leading '0'.

CONFIRMED: overflow is genuinely DETECTED, not wrapped. A hand-rolled accumulate-and-wrap loop is ruled out at both 32-bit and 64-bit width, and atoi() is ruled out, because inputs crafted to land inside 0..65535 after modular reduction still print -1.
CONFIRMED: leading zeros are stripped BEFORE any overflow judgement, i.e. the magnitude, not the digit count, decides. 1000 or 100000 leading zeros do not trigger overflow.
rules.evidence: 'http://h:'+'0'x100000+'/p' -> http/h/0//p/'' (exit 0) ; 'http://h:'+'0'x1000+'65535/p' -> http/h/65535//p/'' ; 'http://h:'+'0'x1000+'65536/p' -> http/h/-1//p/'' ; 'http://h:'+'0'x20+'65535' -> 65535 ; 'http://h:'+'9'x100000+'/p' -> http/h/-1//p/'' (exit 0). rules.rule: CONFIRMED: conversion failure never escapes and never poisons the other four fields. Every pathological port string produced exactly 5 records, exit 0, and empty stderr; the host is still truncated at the colon and path/query are still extracted.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:abc/p?q=1' pattern verified via 'http://h:'+'9'x100000 -> exit=0, outbytes=13, errbytes=0. A 3000-case randomised port fuzz accumulating stderr produced 'stderr bytes total: 0' and 'out_of_contract=0' (no port outside {-1} U [0,65535] ever printed). 'http://h:%2F80' -> http/h/-1/''/'' keeps host 'h'.

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: the port string is bounded by the authority, and the earlier parse steps win. '/', '?', '#' cut the digit run because they end the authority/string, and '@' relocates the colon search entirely.
CONFIRMED: first-colon semantics, and no IPv6 bracket logic, both affect the port exactly as specified.
CONFIRMED: no port without '://'. A colon-digit sequence with no authority separator lands wholly in path with port -1.

SHARPENING (not a divergence, and not parser behaviour): the spec says the only ceiling is 'MAX_ARG_STRLEN ~131072'. The exact boundary is 131071 bytes of argv[1] content. At 131071 the binary runs normally (exit 0, 5 records); at 131072 execve fails with E2BIG so the binary never starts — the shell reports exit 126 and writes to stderr. This is the one place where the spec's blanket claims 'exit status is always 0 whenever argv[1] exists' and 'nothing is ever written to stderr' do not describe the observed process outcome, purely because no process is created.

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: an embedded 0x00 truncates argv at the C-string level before conversion, exactly as the spec describes.
rules.evidence: argv[1] = 'http://h:8\x000' -> http/h/8/''/'' (the trailing '0' is gone, so port is 8 not 80). argv[1] = 'http://h:\x0080' -> http/h/-1/''/'' (port string is empty).

uncertainties: Which failure mechanism produced a given -1 is unobservable. std::stoi throwing std::invalid_argument, std::stoi throwing std::out_of_range (strtol ERANGE), std::out_of_range from the long->int narrowing check, and the explicit `port < 0 || port > 65535` reject all collapse onto the single printed value -1. I could not design any probe that separates them, because every value that would throw is also outside 0..65535. The spec itself acknowledges this; I confirmed it holds for all of 65536, 2147483648, 4294967296, 2^64, 2^128, '-1', 'abc', '' and ' '.

The exact conversion primitive cannot be pinned from output alone. I positively RULED OUT atoi() (4294967296 -> -1, not 0), a wrapping 32-bit accumulator (4294967376 -> -1, not 80; 4295032831 -> -1, not 65535), a wrapping 64-bit accumulator (18446744073709617151 -> -1, not 65535), a digit-count-based overflow heuristic ('0'x1000+'65535' -> 65535), and a full-string-consumed check ('80abc' -> 80). But std::stoi, a hand-written strtol wrapper with its own range check, and an istringstream>>int with a fail() check are mutually indistinguishable.

Whether port_str is authority[colon+1..] or rest[colon+1..] (i.e. whether it extends past the first '/') is undecidable from the 5-line output. Both models are prefixes of each other and strtol stops at '/', which is neither whitespace nor a digit nor a sign. Discriminating probes I designed and ran ('http://h:6/5535' -> 6, 'http://h:80/90' -> 80, 'http://h: /80' -> -1, 'http://h:80x/90' -> 80) give identical results under both models. This is outside my assigned lens but worth flagging.
Port-string absence vs emptiness vs whitespace-only vs sign-only cannot be distinguished from port() alone: 'http://h', 'http://h:', 'http://h:   ', 'http://h:+', 'http://h:-' all print -1.

Whether a trailing-whitespace trim also happens is unobservable: strtol's prefix-parse already ignores everything after the digit run, so ' 80 ' and ' 80' and '80 ' are indistinguishable from a trim-then-convert implementation.

Behaviour for argv[1] longer than 131071 bytes is fundamentally unobservable through this driver (execve returns E2BIG and the binary never runs), so I cannot say whether the parser itself has any internal length ceiling above that point. Everything up to 131071 bytes works with exit 0.

An embedded 0x00 inside the port string cannot be tested as parser input, only as an argv truncation, so I cannot confirm the spec's claim that internal parsing is length-based rather than NUL-terminated for the port field specifically.

0x40 '@' was the sole exception in the 254-byte digit-terminator sweep. I attribute it to STEP 5 userinfo stripping (confirmed by 'http://h:80@9/p' -> host '9'), not to conversion logic, but a reader of the sweep table alone could mistake it for a conversion rule.

Across 59,087 automated differential probes (a byte-exact perl re-implementation of the candidate spec compared against the binary's full 5-line stdout) plus ~260 hand-inspected probes, the candidate spec predicted the binary's output correctly in every single case. Zero mismatches.

rules.rule: SPEC TEXT BUG (prose only, not behavioural): the spec defines find_sub3(s,"://") as "smallest i in [0, len(s)-2]". The correct closed range is [0, len(s)-3], since i+3 must be <= len(s). Taken literally the stated bound reads one byte past the end for the shortest matching strings. Behaviour is unaffected because the real implementation is std::string::find, but an implementer copying the stated bound with unchecked byte reads gets out-of-bounds UB.
rules.evidence: '://' (len 3) must match only at i=0 -> ''/''/-1/''/''; ':/' (len 2) must not match at all -> ''/''/-1/':/'/''. With the stated bound [0,len-2], ':/' would test i=0 reading s[0..3) past the end, and '://' would additionally test i=1 reading s[1..4).

rules.rule: REFINEMENT of the spec's "~131072" argv ceiling: the exact usable limit is 131071 bytes. A 131071-byte relative path round-trips (path printed verbatim); at exactly 131072 bytes execve fails with E2BIG, the program never runs, stdout is 0 bytes, and the shell reports exit 126 with "Argument list too long". So no 5-line output at all is produced -- this is an additional observable outcome the spec's I/O contract ("exactly 5 records whenever argv[1] exists") does not mention.
rules.evidence: 131071 'a's: total stdout 131078 bytes (=131071 path + 7 framing), rc=0. 131072 'a's: rc=126, stdout 0 bytes, stderr 'Argument list too long'. 131070 and 131060 both rc=0.

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: if the fragment- and query-stripped remainder contains no literal 3-byte "://", then scheme='', host='', port=-1 unconditionally, and path = the entire remainder verbatim. Not one input out of ~59k ever produced a non-empty scheme or host, or a port other than -1, in this branch.
CONFIRMED: ':', '/', '@', '\\' are completely inert in the relative branch -- no userinfo strip, no port split, no authority split, no path-vs-authority split, and no default '/' synthesis.

CONFIRMED: the ONLY authority trigger is the contiguous 3-byte sequence 0x3A 0x2F 0x2F. Exhaustive sweeps prove no other 1-, 2-, or 3-byte sequence substitutes: ':'+X+'/' never triggers, ':'+'/'+X never triggers, X+'//' never triggers unless X==':'.
rules.evidence: Sweep b=1..255 over 'a:'+chr(b)+'/b', 'a:/'+chr(b)+'b', 'a'+chr(b)+'//b', 'a:'+chr(b)+chr(b)+'b', 'a'+chr(b)x3+'b', 'h'+chr(b)+'80/p', 'h'+chr(b)+'p'+chr(b)+'q' => 2040 probes, 0 divergences. Plus a full 42x42 pair sweep of interesting bytes in 'a:'+X+Y+'b' and 'a'+X+Y+'b' => 3528 probes, 0 divergences. Concrete: 'a:\t//b' -> ''/''/-1/'a:<09>//b'/''; 'a:/\t/b' -> ''/''/-1/'a:/<09>/b'/''; 'a:%2F%2Fb' -> ''/''/-1/'a:%2F%2Fb'/''.

rules.rule: CONFIRMED (discriminator run): the separator search is std::string::find("://"), NOT find(":") followed by a two-slash check, NOT find("//") followed by a preceding-colon check, and NOT rfind. All three alternative implementations are refuted.
rules.evidence: vs find(':')+check: 'a:b://c' -> 'a:b'/'c'/-1/''/'' (a find(':')-then-check impl would see ':' at index 1, fail the '//' test, and fall to the relative branch giving path 'a:b://c'). vs find('//')+check: 'a//b://c' -> 'a//b'/'c'/-1/''/'' (the first '//' is at index 1 and is not preceded by ':'). vs rfind: 'x://y://z' -> 'x'/'y'/-1/'//z'/'' (rfind would give scheme 'x://y', host 'z').

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: a '/' anywhere before the first "://" does NOT disqualify the scheme -- it just becomes a scheme byte. Many real parsers reject this; this one does not.

CONFIRMED precedence '#' before '?': a '?' that appears after the first '#' produces NO query, which refutes the alternative "query split first" and the alternative "query searched on the raw string".
CONFIRMED: a '?' or '#' occurring before a would-be "://" destroys both scheme and host; with '?', the whole remainder including the "://" lands unparsed in query.
CONFIRMED: no case folding outside the scheme. In the relative branch nothing is lowercased at all, since there is no scheme.
rules.evidence: 'HTTP:A' -> ''/''/-1/'HTTP:A'/''; 'MailTo:X@Y' -> ''/''/-1/'MailTo:X@Y'/''; 'C:/Users/x' -> ''/''/-1/'C:/Users/x'/''. Contrast with the authority branch: 'AB://CD:80/PA?QU' -> 'ab'/'CD'/80/'/PA'/'QU'.

rules.rule: CONFIRMED locale independence (spec claim holds): setting LC_ALL does not change scheme folding, and bytes >=0x80 are never folded.
rules.evidence: Under each of LC_ALL=C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8, POSIX: 'I://X' -> 'i'/'X'/-1/''/''; 'I:X' -> ''/''/-1/'I:X'/''; '\xdd://x' -> '<DD>'/'x'/-1/''/'' (0xDD is 'Y-acute', which would fold in a Latin-1 locale).

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: an empty scheme (leading "://") is legal and distinct from the relative branch. This is the one case where scheme is empty yet host/port/path parsing still runs.
CONFIRMED: a scheme may itself end in or contain ':' -- there is no 'first colon wins' rule for the scheme.
CONFIRMED: only the FIRST "://" is the separator; a later "://" survives verbatim inside path (proving path is not re-scanned).

Corollary (new, spec-implied but unstated): a path produced by the relative branch can NEVER contain "://", while a path produced by the authority branch can.

CONFIRMED: a 0x0A byte in a relative path yields 6 physical output lines, not 5 (fields are raw bytes, not escaped).

rules.rule: CONFIRMED: exit status 0 and empty stderr for every relative/bare-colon input tried; parsing never fails, never throws, never aborts.

uncertainties: No divergence was found, so I cannot report any input where prediction != reality. The honest result of this adversarial pass is that the candidate spec survives ~59,000 differential probes in my lens. The only defects found are a prose off-by-one in the find_sub3 index range ([0,len-2] should be [0,len-3]) and an imprecise argv ceiling ("~131072" -> exactly 131071 usable bytes, with 131072 producing NO output at all).

The spec asserts the no-authority branch also sets fragment and userinfo (and that fragment is stored on the '#' split). These fields are never printed by the driver, so from the 5-line output they are completely unobservable. Any implementation that discards them entirely instead of storing them is indistinguishable.

The spec claims internal parsing is length-based (std::string) rather than NUL-terminated. This is untestable black-box: argv can never deliver a 0x00 byte to the parser (execve truncates first), so the only observable effect is the truncation itself.

Several spec claims are about the binary's contents, not its behaviour, and I did not (per instructions) disassemble or read the binary: the existence of unused trim()/normalize()/normalize_case()/normalize_path()/normalize_query()/is_scheme_valid()/is_host_valid()/is_port_valid()/split_path() functions, the absence of any 'http'/'https' string literal, 65535 being the only port constant, the std::stoi/__gnu_cxx::__stoa call chain, and the LSDA action filter resolving to a bare catch(...). All of these are consistent with observed behaviour but not established by it.

The spec's claim that both std::invalid_argument and std::out_of_range are thrown 'in practice' is not observable: every failure mode collapses onto the single port sentinel -1 with rc=0 and empty stderr, so the two exception types are indistinguishable from outside. (In the relative branch the port is unconditionally -1 anyway, so no port-conversion path is exercised at all there.)

Empty vs absent query, and empty vs absent fragment, are indistinguishable in the 5-line output (spec already says this). Consequently 'a', 'a?', 'a#', 'a?#', 'a#?' are one equivalence class, and '', '#', '?', '#?', '?#' are another. Any spec-equivalent implementation could differ internally here without detection.

I did not exhaustively cover multi-byte sequences longer than 3 bytes as possible alternative authority triggers. I ruled out all 1-byte, all 2-byte (over a 42-byte interesting set plus full 1..255 sweeps in the ':'-adjacent slots), and the 3-byte ':'+X+'/' / ':'+'/'+X / X+'//' families. A hypothetical 4+ byte trigger that never contains '://' remains untested, though the exhaustive {':','/','?','#'} length<=7 sweep (0 divergences) makes one very unlikely.

Behaviour when stdout is a full pipe / closed / non-blocking, and behaviour under a restricted stack for a pathological input, were not probed; they are outside the parsing lens but could in principle produce fewer than 5 records.

result.dimension: Adversarial attack on the candidate spec — lens: IPv6 bracket hosts, userinfo with embedded ":" and "@", and multibyte/high-bit bytes. 52,794 distinct inputs probed. NO DIVERGENCE FOUND.

rules.rule: NO DIVERGENCE FOUND. I implemented the candidate spec exactly as a byte-level reference (/tmp/ref.pl) and diffed its raw 5-record stdout against the real binary over 52,794 distinct inputs in this lens. Mismatches = 0 on every batch. The harness is proven to detect divergence: fed 'http://a\x00b' it correctly flagged PRED host 'a\x00b' vs GOT host 'a' (the argv NUL truncation the spec itself documents as a libc artifact) — that is the ONLY flag raised in the whole campaign.
rules.evidence: Batch results, all via /tmp/cmp.pl (byte-exact raw-stdout compare + exit-status check): hand-written IPv6/userinfo probes 45+46 -> 0 mismatches; exhaustive single-byte sweep 0x01..0xFF x 15 positional templates = 3825 -> 0; curated multibyte/lookalike/invalid-UTF8 set 103 -> 0; random+grammar fuzz 5960 -> 0; second fuzz 11354 -> 0; huge-input set 11 -> 0; EXHAUSTIVE enumeration of all strings of length 1..5 over {':','/','@','[',']','a',0xFF} raw plus length 1..4 with 'http://' prefix = 22407 -> 0; long-string fuzz 9000 -> 0; discriminator batches 27+16 -> 0. Total 52794, mismatches 0.

rules.rule: IPv6 CONFIRMED, sharpened: because the host/port split is find(':') with no bracket awareness, EVERY bracketed IPv6 literal that actually contains ':' collapses the host to the single byte '[' (or to '[' + whatever precedes the first inner colon). The whole address body and the ']' are swallowed into the port string and thrown away.

NEW TRAP the spec does not call out: a bracketed IPv6 URL with NO explicit port can still yield a real port, because the discarded address body is fed to the stoi prefix parse. 'http://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]' yields port 0 (not -1): port string is '0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]', prefix-parses to 0.
rules.evidence: 'http://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]' -> http | [0 | 0 | '' | ''  (port line is '0', not '-1').  Contrast 'http://[::1]' -> port '-1' (port string ':1]' has no leading digit).

rules.rule: A bracket body with no inner ':' behaves as an ordinary host and DOES take a port normally, brackets retained verbatim: host keeps '[' and ']' as plain bytes.
Unbalanced brackets are never repaired or rejected; '[' and ']' are inert bytes anywhere. Bracket-only authorities still produce ports.
']' is an ordinary byte inside the PORT string too, so the stoi prefix parse truncates on it rather than failing: a stray ']' after digits keeps the digits before it.
'/' , '?' and '#' inside brackets terminate/steal the authority exactly as outside them — there is no 'inside brackets' state.

'@' inside brackets is a full userinfo delimiter, which produces hosts with an orphan trailing ']' and can resurrect a valid port. This is the sharpest observable consequence of 'no bracket handling'.
rules.evidence: 'http://[user@host]:80' -> http | host] | 80 | '' | ''.  'http://[a@b]:80' -> http | b] | 80 | '' | ''.  'http://[::1@]:80' -> http | ] | 80 | '' | ''.  Conversely a bracketed literal left of '@' becomes userinfo: 'http://[::1]@x:80' -> http | x | 80 | '' | ''.

rules.rule: USERINFO CONFIRMED: strip is find('@') on the authority only, and the remainder is never re-scanned, so surplus '@' bytes stay in the host.
The port colon is located AFTER the userinfo strip, on the post-'@' text only. Ruled out the alternative 'find first ':' in the whole authority (even left of the '@')' by direct discriminator.
rules.evidence: 'http://u:1@v' -> http | v | -1 | '' | ''  (alternative would give host 'u', port 1).  'http://u:1@v:2@w:3' -> http | v | 2 | '' | ''  (alternative would give host 'u').  'http://a:b@c:d@e:80' -> http | c | -1 | '' | ''.  'http://a:b:c:d@e:f:g:80' -> http | e | -1 | '' | ''.  'http://user:80@a.com' -> http | a.com | -1 | '' | ''.  'http://a.com:80@b.com:90' -> http | b.com | 90 | '' | ''.

rules.rule: The '@' strip happens AFTER the authority/path split, confined to the authority. Ruled out the alternative 'find '@' anywhere in the post-"://" remainder' by direct discriminator.
rules.evidence: 'http://a/b@c' -> http | a | -1 | /b@c | ''  (a global-'@' implementation would give userinfo 'a/b' and host 'c').  'http://a.com/x@y:80' -> http | a.com | -1 | /x@y:80 | ''.  'http://u/v@h:80' -> http | u | -1 | /v@h:80 | ''.  'http://u?v@h:80' -> http | u | -1 | '' | v@h:80.  'http://u#v@h:80' -> http | u | -1 | '' | ''.

rules.rule: An '@' or ':' left of the first "://" is a plain scheme byte and never triggers userinfo/port logic.

MULTIBYTE: all scanning is byte-level with zero encoding awareness. Decisive proof: a delimiter byte occurring as the SECOND byte of a two-byte sequence (Shift-JIS style, where 0x40/0x3A/0x2F/0x3F/0x23 are legal trail bytes) is fully honoured as a delimiter, splitting the multibyte character in half.
rules.evidence: 'http://h\x82\x40x:80' -> http | x | 80 | '' | ''  (the 0x40 acted as userinfo '@').  'http://h\x83\x3Ax:80' -> http | h\x83 | -1 | '' | ''  (0x3A acted as port colon).  'http://h\x84\x2Fx:80' -> http | h\x84 | -1 | /x:80 | ''.  'http://h\x85\x3Fx:80' -> http | h\x85 | -1 | '' | x:80.  'http://h\x86\x23x:80' -> http | h\x86 | -1 | '' | ''.

rules.rule: Conversely, Unicode LOOKALIKES of the delimiters never delimit (no normalization, no confusable folding): FF1A fullwidth colon, FF0F fullwidth solidus, FF20 fullwidth commercial at, FF1F, FF03, FF3B/FF3D fullwidth brackets, U+2044 fraction slash, U+2215 division slash, U+FE55, U+A789 are all inert bytes.

uncertainties: The spec's causal claim "The process never calls setlocale(), so it runs in the C locale no matter what LC_ALL/LC_CTYPE say (verified: LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 still folds 'I'->'i', and 0xA0 is never whitespace)" is NOT verifiable in this container, and the cited evidence is void. I compiled an oracle (/tmp/loc.c, gcc-12): setlocale(LC_ALL,"tr_TR.UTF-8") returns NULL here — the locale does not load, even though `locale -a` lists it. Only C, POSIX, C.UTF-8 and en_US.utf8 actually load. I then scanned every name from `locale -a` (/tmp/scan.c) for a loadable locale whose byte-level tolower or isspace differs from C: there is none (all report tolower_diffs=0 and isspace={09 0A 0B 0C 0D 20}). So 'no setlocale' and 'setlocale + locale-aware tolower' are observationally IDENTICAL in this environment. The behavioural conclusion (C-locale semantics: only 0x41..0x5A fold, only 6 ASCII bytes are port whitespace) is solid; the mechanism is not testable here.

For the same reason, the spec's implementation attributions inside my lens are unfalsifiable: 'C-locale tolower on unsigned char' vs 'tolower on signed char' vs a hand-rolled `if (c>='A'&&c<='Z') c+=32` are byte-for-byte identical for all 255 bytes (my 3825-input exhaustive scheme sweep matched the pure-ASCII model exactly). Likewise the port whitespace skip cannot be distinguished from a hard-coded {09,0A,0B,0C,0D,20} set. Any of these is a valid implementation.

userinfo and fragment are stored but never printed, so every spec sentence about their CONTENT is unobservable through the 5-line output. Only their delimiting effect is testable. An implementation that discards rather than stores userinfo/fragment is indistinguishable. Concretely: 'userinfo = authority[0..at)' is untestable; 'the remainder is not re-scanned for @' IS testable and confirmed ('http://u@v@w' -> host 'v@w').

The spec is silent on encoding awareness as a stated rule — it only says 'no UTF-8 validation' and 'no IDN/punycode'. I found the stronger, decisive fact worth adding explicitly: delimiter bytes occurring as multibyte TRAIL bytes are honoured, splitting characters in half ('http://h\x82\x40x:80' -> host 'x', port 80). Anyone implementing from the spec on a char/codepoint-oriented string type (e.g. Rust String, Python str, Java String) would get this wrong; the spec should state that all five delimiter searches are over raw bytes.

I did not probe the exact kernel MAX_ARG_STRLEN boundary byte-by-byte. I confirmed a ~127 kB argument (126,980 bytes of 0xFE plus 'http://') works with exit 0, consistent with the spec's ~131072 note, but the precise cutoff and its failure mode (execve E2BIG before the process starts) were not characterised.

0x00 cannot be tested as a parser byte at all — it is truncated by execve/argv before the parser runs (my harness flagged exactly this on 'http://a\x00b'). So the spec's claim that internal parsing is length-based rather than NUL-terminated is unverifiable from the outside; it is consistent with, but not proven by, the observations.

result.dimension: Degenerate/empty inputs and inputs consisting only of delimiter characters (adversarial differential test vs. the candidate spec)

rules.rule: NO DIVERGENCE FOUND. I transcribed the candidate spec verbatim into a Perl reference implementation (/tmp/ref.pl, driver /tmp/brute.pl) that byte-compares the reference's expected stdout (5 fields joined by 0x0A + trailing 0x0A) against the real binary's raw stdout AND exit status, and ran ~326,000 differential probes concentrated on degenerate/delimiter-only inputs. Mismatch count was 0 on every batch.

The spec's claim about the empty input is exact, and it extends to every input whose entire content is consumed by fragment truncation or by an empty '://'-authority.
Fragment truncation is TOTAL and unbounded: a leading '#' annihilates arbitrarily large input. A 130001-byte input starting with '#' produces the same 7 output bytes as the empty string.

rules.rule: Delimiter precedence '#' BEFORE '?' is confirmed by degenerate discriminators, and neither truncation ever splices bytes together (so no new '://' can be manufactured).

rules.rule: Repeated '?' : only the first is a delimiter and the remaining ones are literal query bytes, including in the fully degenerate all-'?' case.

An input consisting only of ':' , '/' or '@' bytes (any count, any interleaving that contains no '://') lands entirely in path, verbatim, with scheme='', host='', port=-1, query=''. Confirmed exhaustively for all lengths <= 7 over the 5-delimiter alphabet and up to 130000 bytes.
Exactly +3 consumption after '://' is confirmed in the pure-delimiter case: surplus slashes become the path with an empty host, and a bare '://' leaves an EMPTY path (no synthesized '/').
An empty scheme and a ':'-only or '@'-only scheme are all legal and all trigger authority parsing; tolower is identity on ':' and '@'.

Userinfo stripping genuinely precedes the port colon, and the sharpest witness is a pure-delimiter authority: 'a://h:@' yields host '' (NOT host 'h'), because the '@' strip discards 'h:' first and the remainder has no ':'. A colon-first implementation would print host 'h'.

An empty port string (authority ending in ':') and a whitespace-only port string both give -1, and the isspace set is exactly {09,0A,0B,0C,0D,20} with 0xA0 excluded — verified in the degenerate no-digit form and in the leading-whitespace-then-digits form.
rules.evidence: No-digit -> -1: 'a://h:', 'a://h: ', 'a://h:\x09', 'a://h:\x0a', 'a://h:\x0d', 'a://h:\x0b', 'a://h:\x0c', 'a://h:\xa0', 'a://h:-', 'a://h:+', 'a://h:.', 'a://h:'+(' 'x100000) — all print port -1 with host 'h'. Whitespace accepted before digits: 'a://h: 80' -> 80, 'a://h:\x0a80' -> 80, 'a://h:\x0b80' -> 80. Whitespace after sign rejected: 'a://h:+ 80' -> -1, 'a://h:- 0' -> -1. Double sign rejected: 'a://h:--0' -> -1, 'a://h:-+0' -> -1.

uncertainties: The spec's claims about the FRAGMENT field (fragment = rest[hp+1..]) and the USERINFO field (userinfo = authority[0..at)) are UNOBSERVABLE through this driver, which prints only 5 of the 7 fields. Every degenerate input I tried is consistent with 'fragment/userinfo are discarded outright' just as much as with 'stored in a member'. I can neither confirm nor refute that they are stored, nor whether they are stored with or without their delimiter.

The spec's claim that internal parsing is 'length-based (std::string), not NUL-terminated' and has 'no NUL sensitivity' is not testable via argv: execve/libc truncates argv[1] at the first 0x00 before the parser runs (confirmed: 'a://h:8\x000' -> port 8). No probe in this harness can reach a parser that sees an embedded NUL, so this claim is unfalsifiable here.

Spec text bug (behaviour is right, prose is wrong): find_sub3 is written as 'smallest i in [0, len(s)-2]'. That range is negative for len<3 and off by one for the stated 3-byte slice; it should be [0, len(s)-3]. The observed behaviour matches the corrected bound (':' and ':/' -> no match; '://' -> match at i=0).

Empty vs. absent is fundamentally unobservable for query (both print an empty line 5), for fragment, for userinfo, and for host. Likewise port -1 conflates at least six distinct causes (no ':' in authority, empty port string, whitespace-only, no leading digit, negative magnitude, out of 0..65535). So a large family of degenerate inputs is provably indistinguishable from the empty input: '', '#', '##', '?', '#?', '?#', '#/', '#@', '#://', '#?://a', '?#://a', '://', '://:', '://?', '://#', '://@', '://#a', '\x00' all emit the identical 7 bytes. Any spec rewrite must preserve that collapse but cannot be validated field-by-field on these inputs.

Coverage of long delimiter-only strings is exhaustive only to length 7 over the 5-delimiter alphabet (and length 8 over {':','/','#','?'}, length 14 over {':','/'}). Lengths 9..20 over the full 5-delimiter alphabet were sampled randomly (20000 draws), not exhausted, so a pathological long-string behaviour at, say, length 11 with a specific interleaving would not necessarily have been hit — though the parser's index arithmetic gives no reason to expect one.

Behaviour at or above the kernel MAX_ARG_STRLEN boundary (~131072) is an execve property, not parser logic; I confirmed 130000-byte and 130001-byte delimiter-only argv work (exit 0), but did not bisect the exact ceiling, so the spec's '~131072' figure is unverified in detail.
